Blaise Pascal
Steve Wozniak

The Transistor

The Pascaline
The Stepped Reckoner
The Difference Engine

The Singer Loom
The Gutenberg Press

options: Vacuum tubes
Integrated circuits
Microprocessors
Transistors

options: The Optical Laser
The Microprocessor
The Transistor
The Magnetic Tape

1.question: What electronic component defined third-generation computers by combining thousands of transistors on a single silicon chip?
options: The Integrated Circuit (IC)
The Mechanical Relay
The Floppy Disk
The Vacuum Tube

options: The CRT Display
The Punch Card
The Vacuum Tube
The Microprocessor

1.question: What was the name of the first general-purpose electronic digital computer completed in the US in 1945?
options: UNIVAC
Apple I
ENIAC
EDVAC

1.question: What was the first commercially produced digital computer sold to the US Census Bureau in 1951?
options: IBM 360
UNIVAC I
Altair 8800
ENIAC

1.question: What observation stated that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles roughly every two years?
options: Moore's Law
Turing's Law
Shannon's Law
Metcalfe's Law

options: Von Neumann Architecture
Harvard Architecture
Babbage Design
Turing Architecture

1.question: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN in Switzerland?
options: Bill Gates
Tim Berners-Lee
Steve Jobs
Vint Cerf

options: ETHERNET
BITNET
NSFNET
ARPANET

Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak
Bill Gates and Paul Allen
Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn

options: Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak
Larry Page and Sergey Brin
Bill Gates and Paul Allen

options: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie
Mark Zuckerberg and Eduardo Saverin
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak
Bill Gates and Paul Allen

options: Bjarne Stroustrup
Guido van Rossum
Dennis Ritchie
James Gosling

options: Tim Berners-Lee

Linus Torvalds
Ken Thompson

options: Larry Ellison
Richard Stallman
Steve Ballmer
Linus Torvalds

options: NCSA Mosaic
Mozilla Firefox
Google Chrome
Internet Explorer

1.question: What is the difference between computer science and computer literacy?

Computer science studies computational theory, design, and programming, while computer literacy is the ability to use software tools
Computer literacy requires writing machine code

1.question: What is information theory, founded by Claude Shannon in 1948?
options: The legal study of patent ownership
The history of physical libraries
The science of building plastic computer cases
The mathematical study of the quantification, storage, compression, and communication of digital data

The Colossus

options: UNIVAC

A build-it-yourself microcomputer kit that catalyzed the hobbyist personal computer movement
The first smartphone with internet connectivity
A high-speed laser printer

1.question: What is an algorithm in computer science?
options: A high-speed network cable
A precise, finite sequence of unambiguous instructions to solve a specific problem
A virus that corrupts computer data
A piece of hardware soldered inside a power supply

1.question: What is computational thinking?
options: A problem-solving approach that formulates problems so their solutions can be represented as computational algorithms
Typing at more than 100 words per minute
Memorizing binary numbers from 0 to 1,000
Building physical desktop computer towers

options: The historical period characterized by the rapid shift from traditional industry to an economy based on information technology
The era before paper was invented
The period when steam engines powered factories
The time when electricity was first discovered

1.question: What does the acronym CPU stand for?

Computer Power Unit
Central Peripheral User
Core Program Utility

1.question: What does GUI stand for in computer interface history?
options: Global Universal Internet
General User Instruction
Gigabit Upload Interface
Graphical User Interface

Bell Labs
Apple Cupertino
Xerox PARC (Palo Alto Research Center)

options: Douglas Engelbart
Alan Kay
Bill Gates
Steve Jobs

options: Wide Yield Screen Interface Window Guide
What You See Is What You Get
Word Yielding Simple Indexed Writing Graph
When You See It Work Gently

1.question: What is open-source software?
options: Software that costs more than one thousand dollars
Software that cannot run without an internet connection
Software whose source code is freely available for inspection, modification, and redistribution
Software owned exclusively by the government
1.explanation: Open-source software promotes community collaboration and transparency.

1.question: What is proprietary (closed-source) software?
options: Software written by elementary school students
Software that has no copyright and belongs to everyone
Software whose source code is private, copyrighted, and owned by a commercial company (e.g., Windows)
Software that only works on printers

1.question: What does RAM stand for in computer memory?
options: Read All Memory
Remote Access Mechanism
Random Access Memory
Rapid Action Module
1.explanation: RAM provides fast, temporary volatile storage for active processes.

1.question: What is the primary characteristic of volatile computer memory?
options: It stores data permanently for decades
It loses all stored data when electrical power is turned off
It cannot be accessed by the CPU
It can only be read by laser beams
1.explanation: RAM is volatile; data vanishes without continuous electrical refresh.

1.question: What does ROM stand for in computer hardware?
options: Real Operating Module
Random Optical Media
Read-Only Memory
Remote Online Memory
1.explanation: ROM contains permanent, non-volatile startup firmware (BIOS/UEFI).

1.question: What is cloud computing in modern technology?
options: A physical antenna placed on a roof
Running computers exclusively on rainy days
Delivering computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking) over the Internet on demand
Storing files directly on smartphone screens
1.explanation: Cloud computing provides scalable off-premises compute and storage.

1.question: What is a supercomputer?
options: A high-performance computing system engineered to perform trillions of calculations per second for scientific simulations
A printer that prints ten pages per minute
A smartphone that has an extra-long battery life
A standard desktop PC running a video game
1.explanation: Supercomputers solve complex scientific, meteorological, and cryptographic problems.

1.question: What is quantum computing in emerging computer science?
options: Computing that leverages quantum mechanical phenomena (superposition and entanglement) to solve complex problems
Computing using small plastic beads
Connecting monitors with optical glass
Running software without any electricity
1.explanation: Quantum computers use qubits to process exponentially vast calculation states.

1.question: What is an embedded system?
options: A laptop running multiple operating systems
A dedicated computer system designed to perform a dedicated function within a larger machine (e.g., microwave, ABS brakes)
A desktop computer used in an office
A server housed in a commercial data center

1.question: What is artificial intelligence (AI) in computer science?
options: A high-speed wireless home internet router
A mechanical robot with physical muscles
A computer monitor that displays 3D movies
The simulation of human intelligence processes by computer systems, such as learning, reasoning, and self-correction
1.explanation: AI enables software to emulate human perception, problem-solving, and decision-making.

1.question: What is cybersecurity?
options: The practice of protecting systems, networks, and programs from digital attacks and unauthorized access
Building physical desktop computer cases
Cleaning dust from cooling fans
Writing code for video games
1.explanation: Cybersecurity safeguards confidentiality, integrity, and availability of digital assets.

1.question: Why is studying computer science foundational for students in the 21st century?
options: It fosters analytical thinking, problem-solving skills, and empowers students to shape the digital technologies driving the world
It replaces the need to learn math or science
It forces students to work exclusively in computer factories
It guarantees that students will never have to pay taxes
1.explanation: Computer science literacy prepares students to innovate and participate in an automated digital society.

2.question: What is the central printed circuit board that connects all components of a computer system?
options: The Optical Drive
The Sound Card
The Power Supply
The Motherboard
2.explanation: The motherboard serves as the main circuit spine connecting CPU, RAM, and storage.

2.question: What socket on the motherboard houses the microprocessor chip?
options: The PCIe Slot
The CPU Socket
The DIMM Slot
The SATA Port

2.question: What slots on the motherboard hold RAM modules?
options: M.2 Slots
DIMM Slots
PCIe Slots
SATA Ports

2.question: What high-speed expansion slot is primarily used for dedicated graphics cards and NVMe adapters?
options: IDE
ISA
PCIe (PCI Express)
AGP

2.question: What does the chipest on a motherboard do?
options: It displays text and images on the monitor screen
It manages data communications between the CPU, RAM, storage, and peripheral expansion buses
It converts AC electricity to DC electricity
It cools the processor using liquid coolant
2.explanation: The chipset directs data traffic between the processor and system peripherals.

2.question: What component inside the CPU performs arithmetic calculations (addition, subtraction) and logical comparisons (AND, OR)?
options: The System Clock
The Control Unit
The Register Bank
The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)
2.explanation: The ALU carries out arithmetic and logic operations in the processor.

2.question: What component inside the CPU coordinates instruction fetching, decoding, and directs data flow?
options: The Arithmetic Logic Unit
The Control Unit (CU)
The Heat Sink
The Expansion Bus

2.question: What are the small, ultra-fast internal storage cells located directly inside the CPU called?
options: Hard platters
Registers
Flash drives
RAM sticks

2.question: What is CPU cache memory?
options: A cloud server located in a remote data center
Permanent storage for video files on the hard drive
High-speed SRAM located on the CPU chip to hold frequently accessed data and instructions
A liquid coolant running across silicon chips
2.explanation: Cache memory (L1, L2, L3) accelerates access to frequently requested memory words.

2.question: In the CPU cache hierarchy, which level is the fastest and closest to the processor cores?
options: L2 Cache
L1 Cache
L3 Cache
RAM
2.explanation: L1 cache is the smallest, fastest memory tier integrated directly into core execution units.

2.question: What does the clock speed of a CPU (measured in GHz) represent?
options: The number of clock cycles the processor can execute per second
The speed of the cooling fans in RPM
The total storage capacity of the hard drive
The physical weight of the computer tower
2.explanation: Clock speed (e.g., 3.8 GHz = 3.8 billion cycles/second) benchmarks processor cycle frequency.

2.question: What is a multi-core processor?
options: A motherboard with two power supplies
A single computing component with two or more independent processing units (cores) that execute instructions concurrently
A processor with two cooling fans
A monitor with four display screens
2.explanation: Multi-core processors enable true parallel processing across separate hardware cores.

2.question: What is the continuous cycle the CPU performs to run programs?
options: The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
The Input-Process-Display Cycle
The Boot-Reboot-Shutdown Cycle
The Read-Write-Format Cycle
2.explanation: The CPU continuously fetches instructions from RAM, decodes their opcode, and executes them.

A communication pathway consisting of electrical traces that transfers data and signals between computer components
A power cable plugged into a wall socket
A software program that speeds up internet downloads
2.explanation: Buses transmit address, control, and data signals across motherboard components.

2.question: What are the three main types of system buses in computer architecture?
options: Audio Bus, Video Bus, and Network Bus
USB Bus, SATA Bus, and PCIe Bus
Primary Bus, Secondary Bus, and Tertiary Bus
Data Bus, Address Bus, and Control Bus
2.explanation: System architecture divides buses into data lines, memory address lines, and control signals.

2.question: What does the Power Supply Unit (PSU) do in a desktop computer?
options: It generates electricity from solar energy
It converts household alternating current (AC) into low-voltage direct current (DC) required by internal components
It cools the graphics card using compressed air
It stores files permanently when power is turned off
2.explanation: The PSU steps down AC wall power into regulated +12V, +5V, and +3.3V DC rails.

2.question: What is the purpose of thermal paste applied between a CPU and its heat sink?
options: To conduct electricity into the processor pins
To make the computer run completely silently
To fill microscopic air gaps and facilitate efficient heat transfer from the processor to the cooler
To glue the CPU permanently so it cannot be removed
2.explanation: Thermal paste eliminates insulating air pockets, maximizing thermal conductivity.

Speeding up fans until they break
Automatically reducing CPU clock speed to decrease heat output when temperature limits are reached
Shutting down the monitor screen to save energy
2.explanation: Thermal throttling protects silicon dies from permanent heat damage by lowering clock speeds.

2.question: How does a Solid-State Drive (SSD) differ from a traditional Hard Disk Drive (HDD)?

HDDs are 100 times faster than SSDs
SSDs use non-volatile flash memory chips with no moving parts, while HDDs use spinning magnetic platters
SSDs lose all data when power is turned off

A backup tape used by corporate mainframes
A memory card used exclusively in digital cameras

Uniform Software Backup

United System Binary

High-Definition Multimedia Interface
Home Digital Media Integration
Host Device Memory Interconnect

DVI

Connecting computers to high-refresh-rate, high-resolution digital computer monitors
Connecting desktop computers to wall power sockets
Connecting speakers to analog audio jacks

A cable that plugs into a wall outlet
A hardware component that enables a computer to connect to a network (via Ethernet or Wi-Fi)
A card that plays music through speakers

MAC Address (Media Access Control)

IP Address

Binary Integrated Operating System
Boot Initialized Output Software
Base Internal Optical Storage

options: CMOS
POST
UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)
ACPI

The Solar Rechargeable Cell
The CMOS Battery (CR2032)
The Power Supply Capacitor

Primary Output System Terminal
Permanent Optical Storage Track
Power-On Self-Test

A technician who delivers computers to homes

A screwdriver used to build computer cases

2.question: What is hardware form factor in desktop computing?

The standardized physical size, shape, and layout of motherboards, power supplies, and cases (e.g., ATX, Micro-ATX)
The software operating system installed
The price of computer parts in retail stores

2.question: What does overclocking a CPU or GPU mean?

Allowing the computer to run for 24 hours straight
Configuring the component to run at a higher clock speed than its factory-rated specification to gain performance
Placing a clock on top of the computer case

2.question: What is the primary danger of excessive computer component overclocking without adequate cooling?

Component instability, system crashes, and permanent silicon degradation from overheating
The monitor screen breaking physically
The hard drive catching fire immediately

2.question: What is static electricity (Electrostatic Discharge / ESD) risk when assembling computer hardware?

Dust accumulating on computer cooling fans
Getting an electric shock that trips the house circuit breaker
A sudden surge of static electricity from a human hand that can permanently fry sensitive silicon microchips

2.question: What tool is recommended to dissipate static electricity when building or upgrading PC components?

A pair of thick wool mittens
An anti-static wrist strap connected to an unpainted grounded metal surface
A wooden stick held in the left hand
2.explanation: Grounded anti-static wrist straps safely drain human electrostatic charges.

A virus program that attacks computer hard drives

A power cord that never tangles

The Desktop GUI
The Kernel
The Shell

There is no difference between them

A printed user manual for software

options: A cable powering the cooling fan
A line of text written in a document
A physical cord inside an Ethernet cable
The smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be managed independently by an OS scheduler

options: The ability of the operating system to execute multiple tasks or processes concurrently
Connecting two monitors to one computer
Installing three different web browsers
Typing on two keyboards simultaneously

3.question: What is preemptive scheduling in an operating system?
options: Processes choose when they want to stop running
All processes run on separate physical computers
The OS scheduler can interrupt and suspend a running process to allocate CPU time to another higher-priority process
The computer restarts whenever a program finishes

Switching between dark mode and light mode on the screen
Changing the desktop background wallpaper
Saving the state of a currently running process so it can be resumed later, and loading the state of another process

3.question: What is a deadlock in operating systems?
options: A computer monitor that turns black
A broken wire inside the computer power supply
A situation where two or more processes are unable to proceed because each is waiting for a resource held by the other
A virus that locks the user out with a password

3.question: What is virtual memory in an operating system?
options: A memory chip that only exists in virtual reality
A memory management technique that uses secondary storage (disk space) to extend physical RAM
A cloud server that backs up personal files
A RAM stick made of optical glass

Scanning documents into PDF format
Sending messages across a digital network
Writing numbers on physical sheets of paper

A printer running out of physical paper
A broken pixel on a computer monitor
A software syntax error in Python code

A high-speed graphics rendering technique
Cleaning dust out of cooling fans
A catastrophic state where the OS spends more time swapping memory pages in and out of disk than executing real instructions
3.explanation: Thrashing occurs when memory demand exceeds physical RAM, causing constant page faulting.

3.question: What is a file system in an operating system?

A physical metal cabinet storing office papers
A web browser used to visit search engines
The method and data structure used by an OS to organize, name, store, and locate files on storage drives

options: NTFS (New Technology File System)
ext4
FAT32
APFS

options: APFS (Apple File System)
FAT16
exFAT
NTFS

3.question: Which journaling file system is widely used as the default for Linux distributions (like Ubuntu)?
options: ext4
FAT32
HFS+
NTFS

NTFS
FAT32
ext4

NTFS
ZFS
FAT16

A list of employee phone numbers in an office
A special web page on the internet
A physical drawer inside a desk

3.question: What is the difference between an absolute path and a relative path to a file?
options: An absolute path only works on Windows computers

An absolute path specifies the complete location from the root directory, while a relative path starts from the current working directory
A relative path cannot contain folder names

options: Colon (:)
Backslash (\)
Forward slash (/)
Tilde (~)

options: C: (C drive)
A: drive
B: drive
Z: drive

3.question: What does a file extension (such as .docx, .png, .py) indicate to the operating system?

The format and type of file, indicating which application should open it
The physical factory where the computer was made
The author's legal name who wrote the document

3.question: What is file metadata?
options: The plastic label glued on a hard drive
The main text content written inside a story
The electrical voltage of the computer monitor
Descriptive data about a file, such as its size, creation date, modification timestamp, author, and access permissions

A fee paid to save documents on the desktop
A permit required to buy a computer from a store

Restore, Window, and eXplore
Reboot, Wipe, and eXit
Read, Write, and Execute permissions

chown
mkdir
chmod

dir
cd
ls

3.question: What command in Linux and Windows command lines changes the current working directory?
options: rm
cp
mv
cd (change directory)

3.question: What command prints the current working directory path in a Linux/Unix terminal?
options: where
dir
path
pwd (print working directory)

3.question: What is an interrupt in computer operating systems?
options: A typo made while writing software code
A user unplugging the computer mouse
A hardware or software signal that prompts the CPU to temporarily halt current execution to handle an urgent event
A power outage that causes a blackout

options: A website that answers computer questions
A program that checks the computer for dust
A physical cable connecting the mouse
A specialized software routine invoked by the OS to handle a specific hardware or software interrupt

options: An advertisement displayed on a web browser
The programmatic method by which an application requests a service from the operating system kernel (e.g., file I/O)
A sound effect played when opening a folder
A telephone call made between computer engineers

3.question: What is user mode versus kernel mode in CPU protection rings?

User mode is for adults and kernel mode is for children
User mode runs applications with restricted hardware access, while kernel mode runs the OS with full, unrestricted access to all hardware

A screwdriver used to build computer cases
A hardware cable connecting the monitor

Wiping the hard drive clean of all files
Polishing the physical surface of a disk platter

SSDs only work on Linux computers

Deleting old files to save disk space

3.question: What is the well-known '3-2-1 Backup Strategy' recommended by IT professionals?

Backup data every 3 hours, 2 days a week, for 1 year

A high-speed graphics rendering engine

Binary is easier for human beings to read than base 10

Translating English into Spanish

A compression method that never deletes any data

An error that occurs when a mathematical calculation produces a value larger than the maximum value representable by the allocated number of bits

options: Alan Turing

A gate that adds two binary bits
A gate that outputs 1 when any input is 1
