The Storage Platter
7.explanation: The call stack pushes activation records on calls and pops them on returns.

7.question: What error occurs when a program pushes more data onto the call stack than the allocated memory can hold?
options: Syntax Error
Stack Underflow
Stack Overflow
Memory Division Error
7.explanation: Excessive stack frames (e.g., infinite recursion) cause stack overflow crashes.

7.question: What error occurs when a program attempts to pop an element from an empty stack?
options: Out of Bounds Error
Stack Overflow
Type Error
Stack Underflow
7.explanation: Popping from an empty stack triggers a stack underflow condition.

7.question: What is a Queue data structure?
options: A linear data structure that follows the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle
A Last-In, First-Out stack
An unordered set of keys
A table with rows and columns
7.explanation: Queues follow FIFO: the first item inserted is the first one removed.

7.question: What real-world analogy best describes a Queue data structure?
options: A line of customers waiting at a grocery checkout counter
A deck of playing cards shuffled randomly
A dictionary of words
A stack of heavy books on a desk
7.explanation: Customers who arrive first in line are served first (FIFO).

7.question: What queue operation adds an element to the rear (end) of the queue?
options: Pop
Enqueue
Peek
Dequeue
7.explanation: Enqueue inserts an element at the back of the queue.

7.question: What queue operation removes and returns the element from the front (head) of the queue?
options: Insert
Push
Enqueue
Dequeue
7.explanation: Dequeue extracts the front element from the queue.

7.question: Which computing system utilizes a queue to manage print jobs sent by multiple users?
options: A web browser bookmark manager
A print spooler
A computer power supply
A CPU cache controller
7.explanation: Print spoolers process print jobs in FIFO order via a print queue.

7.question: What is a circular queue in data structures?
options: A queue that runs in reverse order
A queue where the last position is connected back to the first position to make efficient use of fixed memory buffers
A queue that has no beginning or end
A queue used only for drawing circles
7.explanation: Circular queues reuse vacated front spaces in ring buffers without shifting elements.

7.question: What is a Priority Queue?
options: A queue that charges users money to jump ahead
A stack that only stores integers
A list that is sorted alphabetically
An abstract data structure where each element has an associated priority, and elements with higher priority are dequeued before lower priority elements
7.explanation: Emergency rooms and OS schedulers use priority queues to service high-priority tasks first.

7.question: What is a Linked List?
options: An array stored contiguously in memory
A linear collection of data elements (nodes) where each node points to the next node in memory via a pointer or reference
A table with fixed columns and rows
A set of numbers saved on a USB drive
7.explanation: Linked lists chain dynamically allocated nodes linked by pointer references.

7.question: What two components comprise an individual node in a singly linked list?
options: An integer and a float
A username and a password
Data (payload) and a pointer/reference to the next node
A row and a column
7.explanation: Each node holds its data value plus a link pointer to the successor node.

7.question: What does the 'head' of a linked list represent?
options: The length of the list in bytes
The middle element of the list
A reference or pointer to the very first node in the list
The last node in the list
7.explanation: The head pointer anchors the beginning of linked list traversal.

7.question: What does the 'next' pointer of the final node in a singly linked list point to?
options: The middle node
Null (or None), signaling the end of the list
A random memory address
The head node
7.explanation: A null pointer marks the terminal end of a linear linked list.

7.question: What is a Doubly Linked List?
options: A list that has twice as many elements
A list that stores two data values per node
A list that cannot be edited
A linked list where each node contains pointers to BOTH the next node and the previous node
7.explanation: Bidirectional pointers permit forward and backward list traversal.

7.question: What is a major advantage of a linked list over a static array?
options: Faster random access by index number
Using less total memory per element
Dynamic sizing: elements can be inserted and deleted without reallocating or shifting the entire array
Immunity from computer viruses
7.explanation: Linked lists grow dynamically without expensive array resizing operations.

7.question: What is a major disadvantage of a linked list compared to an array?
options: No instantaneous random access (O(n) sequential traversal required to reach the nth element)
Inability to store string text
Requires an internet connection to run
Inability to add elements at the beginning
7.explanation: Accessing index k requires traversing k pointers from the head: O(k).

7.question: What is a Hash Table (Hash Map)?
options: A physical wooden table with computers
A stack that only stores text strings
A data structure that stores key-value pairs and uses a hash function to compute index locations for rapid retrieval
A sorted alphabetical list of words
7.explanation: Hash tables provide average O(1) dictionary lookups via mathematical hashing.

7.question: What is a hash function in a hash table?
options: A function that translates code into Spanish
A function that deletes duplicate files
A function that converts a search key into an integer index within the internal bucket array
A function that prints receipts
7.explanation: Hash functions map arbitrary key strings into array index offsets.

7.question: What is a hash collision in a hash table?
options: When two computers have the same IP address
When a computer screen turns off
When a hard drive physically crashes
A situation where two different search keys produce the exact same array index from the hash function
7.explanation: Collisions occur when hash(key1) == hash(key2) for distinct keys.

7.question: What is chaining (separate chaining) in hash collision resolution?
options: Multiplying the hash index by two
Maintaining a linked list of all key-value entries that hash to the same bucket index
Deleting both keys when a collision happens
Restarting the computer operating system
7.explanation: Chaining appends colliding records into linked lists attached to bucket slots.

7.question: What is the average-case time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion in a well-designed hash table?
options: O(log n) - Logarithmic time
O(1) - Constant time
O(n) - Linear time
O(n^2) - Quadratic time
7.explanation: Hash tables achieve near-instantaneous O(1) average performance.

7.question: What is a Tree data structure in computer science?
options: A physical wooden computer component
A non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges, starting from a single root node
A circular ring of memory buffers
A linear list of numbers in order
7.explanation: Trees organize hierarchical data (like file systems and DOMs).

7.question: What is the top node of a tree data structure called?
options: The Branch node
The Root node
The Base node
The Leaf node
7.explanation: The root is the ancestral origin node having no parent.

7.question: What are nodes in a tree that have no child nodes called?
options: Leaf nodes (or terminal nodes)
Parent nodes
Root nodes
Branch nodes
7.explanation: Leaves reside at tree extremities with null child pointers.

7.question: What is a Binary Tree?
options: A tree data structure where each node has at most TWO children (referred to as left child and right child)
A tree that has no leaves
A tree that has two root nodes
A tree that only stores binary 0s and 1s
7.explanation: Binary trees restrict child branching to a maximum of two per node.

7.question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
options: A tree that cannot be searched
A binary tree where the left subtree contains values LESS than the node, and the right subtree contains values GREATER than the node
A tree where all leaves have identical values
A tree where nodes are placed randomly
7.explanation: The BST ordering property enables logarithmic O(log n) search and insertion.

7.question: What is the average-case time complexity to search for a value in a balanced Binary Search Tree?
options: O(n^2) - Quadratic time
O(n) - Linear time
O(1) - Constant time
O(log n) - Logarithmic time
7.explanation: Balanced BSTs halve remaining candidate nodes at each level.

7.question: What is a Graph data structure in computer science?
options: A non-linear data structure consisting of a finite set of vertices (nodes) and a set of edges connecting them
A bar chart displaying company profits
A line graph showing daily temperatures
A pie chart showing market shares
7.explanation: Graphs model network relationships (social networks, road maps, web links).

7.question: What are the two fundamental components that define a Graph: G = (V, E)?
options: Variables and Execution
Vertices (nodes) and Edges (connections)
Values and Equations
Vectors and Entities
7.explanation: Graphs comprise vertices representing entities and edges representing relationships.

7.question: What is an undirected graph versus a directed graph (digraph)?
options: Undirected graphs have no nodes
Directed graphs only work on computers
There is no difference between them
In an undirected graph edges are bidirectional, while in a directed graph edges have a specific direction from one vertex to another
7.explanation: Directed edges represent one-way relationships (like Twitter followers).

7.question: What is a weighted graph?
options: A graph where each edge has an assigned numerical value (weight) representing cost, distance, or capacity
A graph that only contains integers
A graph that weighs five pounds on a scale
A graph that has heavy lines drawn on paper
7.explanation: Weighted edges model distances or costs (like highway mileages between cities).

7.question: What classic pathfinding algorithm finds the shortest path between nodes in a weighted graph?
options: Dijkstra's Algorithm
Linear Search
Binary Search
Bubble Sort
7.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm finds optimal shortest paths in non-negative weighted graphs.

7.question: What graph traversal algorithm explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking?
options: Depth-First Search (DFS)
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Binary Search
Linear Search
7.explanation: DFS uses a stack (or recursion) to traverse deep down paths before backtracking.

7.question: What graph traversal algorithm explores all neighboring vertices at the current depth before moving to the next depth level?
options: Depth-First Search (DFS)
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Merge Search
Bubble Search
7.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue to explore nodes in concentric wavefront levels.

7.question: Why is choosing the appropriate data structure essential in software engineering?
options: It makes computers physically lighter
It prevents programmers from having to write code
It ensures that no computer bugs can ever happen
It directly impacts the execution speed, memory consumption, and algorithmic efficiency of the application
7.explanation: Data structure selection dictates runtime performance and resource scaling.

8.question: What is a computer network?
options: A printer cable disconnected from a computer
A monitor displaying high-definition video
A single laptop running on battery power
A collection of interconnected computing devices that can exchange data and share resources
8.explanation: Networks connect autonomous computers to facilitate communication and resource sharing.

8.question: What does LAN stand for in networking?
options: Large Access Network
Logical Array Node
Local Area Network
Linked Application Network
8.explanation: LAN connects devices in a localized area such as a school, office, or home.

8.question: What does WAN stand for in networking?
options: Wireless Access Node
World Audio Node
Web Application Network
Wide Area Network
8.explanation: WAN spans broad geographical distances (the Internet is the preeminent WAN).

8.question: What is a PAN (Personal Area Network)?
options: A network of underwater ocean sensors
A computer network installed on airplanes
A nationwide network connecting government offices
A small network centered around an individual person within a range of a few meters (e.g., Bluetooth devices)
8.explanation: PAN connects personal wearables, headphones, and mobile devices over short ranges.

8.question: What does WLAN stand for?
options: Web Linked Application Network
Wide Line Access Node
World Layer Audio Network
Wireless Local Area Network
8.explanation: WLAN uses radio frequencies (like Wi-Fi) to connect devices locally without cables.

8.question: What is network topology?
options: The speed of the network router in megabits
The operating system used on network servers
The price of network cables in stores
The physical or logical arrangement and layout of devices and connections in a computer network
8.explanation: Topology maps node layout and communication links in a network.

8.question: In a Star network topology, how are all network devices connected?
options: Every device connects to every other device directly
All devices connect to a single central backbone cable
Each individual device connects directly to a central hub, switch, or router
Each device connects to exactly two neighbors forming a closed ring
8.explanation: Star topologies link all endpoints to a central switch; failure of one cable affects only that node.

8.question: What is a major advantage of a Star network topology?
options: If one connection cable fails, only that individual device is disconnected; the rest of the network operates normally
It can never be hacked by viruses
It requires zero cables to set up
It eliminates the need for network switches
8.explanation: Centralized star switching isolates peripheral link failures.

8.question: In a Bus network topology, how are devices connected?
options: All devices connect to a central wireless satellite
Devices are connected with no wires
All devices share and connect to a single central backbone cable with terminators at both ends
Each device connects to two other devices in a circle
8.explanation: Bus topologies use a shared linear transmission line terminated at both ends.

8.question: What happens in a Bus network topology if the main backbone cable breaks?
options: The entire network stops functioning completely
The network automatically doubles its speed
The computers switch to satellite radio
Only one computer loses connection
8.explanation: A backbone break destroys electrical termination, halting all bus communications.

8.question: In a Ring network topology, how are devices connected?
options: Devices are arranged in a straight vertical line
Each device connects to exactly two neighboring devices, forming a continuous circular loop for data
Every device connects to five other computers
All devices connect to a central wall socket
8.explanation: Ring topologies pass tokens or packets sequentially around a closed circuit.

8.question: What is a Mesh network topology?
options: A network arranged in a triangle shape
A network where only one computer can talk at a time
A network where devices are interconnected with multiple redundant links (full mesh connects all nodes to all other nodes)
A network that operates without electricity
8.explanation: Mesh topologies provide high fault tolerance via multiple redundant routing pathways.

8.question: What is a major advantage of a Full Mesh network topology?
options: High redundancy and reliability: if one link fails, traffic can be rerouted through alternative paths
It is the cheapest network to build
It can only connect two devices total
It requires the fewest cables of any topology
8.explanation: Redundant pathways prevent single points of failure across mesh architectures.

8.question: What is packet switching in digital networks?
options: Switching between wired and wireless connections
Turning network switches off and on rapidly
Breaking messages into small packets, routing them independently across the network, and reassembling them at the destination
Replacing old Ethernet cables with fiber optics
8.explanation: Packet switching dynamically routes discrete data packets across shared network paths.

8.question: What does an individual network packet contain besides its data payload?
options: A copy of the operating system kernel
An invoice for network service fees
A digital video recording of the user
Header information including source IP address, destination IP address, packet sequence number, and error checks
8.explanation: Packet headers encapsulate routing, addressing, and sequencing metadata.

8.question: What is the role of a Router in computer networking?
options: It cools desktop processors with air fans
It displays web pages on computer monitors
It converts digital audio into analog sound waves
It inspects destination IP addresses on data packets and forwards them between different networks along the best route
8.explanation: Routers operate at Layer 3 (Network), interconnecting disparate network subnets.

8.question: What does a network Switch do in a Local Area Network (LAN)?
options: It connects local computers directly to space satellites
It provides electrical power to wall outlets
It translates domain names into IP addresses
It connects devices within the same local network and uses MAC addresses to forward data frames directly to the intended device
8.explanation: Switches operate at Layer 2 (Data Link), filtering and directing frames via MAC tables.

8.question: How does a network Switch differ from an older legacy network Hub?
options: A hub uses laser beams instead of cables
A hub is faster and more secure than a switch
A switch forwards data only to the specific intended port, while a hub broadcasts data to all connected ports indiscriminately
A switch connects only two computers total
8.explanation: Switches prevent collision domains by directing traffic intelligently to target MACs.

8.question: What does a Modem do in home Internet connectivity?
options: It stores files permanently on disk
It prints web pages onto paper
It modulates and demodulates signals, converting analog signals from an ISP into digital signals a router can understand
It monitors room temperature
8.explanation: Modems convert between ISP transmission media signals and digital Ethernet.

8.question: What is the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) reference model?
options: A software program that speeds up internet downloads
A physical cable used to connect servers
A federal law regulating computer sales
A conceptual architectural framework that describes network functions in seven distinct hierarchical layers
8.explanation: The 7-layer OSI model standardizes network communication protocols.

8.question: How many layers are in the standard OSI model?
options: 7 layers
4 layers
5 layers
10 layers
8.explanation: The OSI model consists of 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

8.question: Which layer is Layer 1 (the lowest layer) of the OSI model?
options: Data Link Layer
Physical Layer
Network Layer
Application Layer
8.explanation: Layer 1 handles raw bit transmission over physical media (cables, radio waves).

8.question: Which layer is Layer 7 (the highest layer) of the OSI model, interacting directly with user software?
options: Session Layer
Application Layer
Network Layer
Transport Layer
8.explanation: Layer 7 provides network services directly to user applications (HTTP, FTP, DNS).

8.question: What does TCP/IP stand for?
options: Transfer Control Packet / Interactive Portal
Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol
Total Computer Processing / Interface Program
Terminal Communication Path / Internal Protocol
8.explanation: TCP/IP is the foundational protocol suite underpinning the global Internet.

8.question: What does an IP address (Internet Protocol address) do?
options: It uniquely identifies a device connected to an IP network, enabling routing and addressing
It specifies the user's secret password
It measures the speed of the processor in gigahertz
It identifies the brand of the computer monitor
8.explanation: IP addresses provide logical network addressing for global packet routing.

8.question: What is the format of an IPv4 address?
options: Six letters separated by dashes
Four decimal numbers separated by dots (periods), ranging from 0 to 255 (e.g., 192.168.1.1)
A single 32-digit binary string
Eight hexadecimal words separated by colons
8.explanation: IPv4 uses 32 bits arranged in 4 dotted-decimal octets.

8.question: How many total bits make up an IPv4 address?
options: 16 bits
64 bits
32 bits
128 bits
8.explanation: IPv4 addresses consist of 32 bits, allowing approximately 4.3 billion addresses.

8.question: Why was IPv6 developed to replace IPv4?
options: IPv4 was outlawed by international treaty
IPv4's 32-bit address pool became exhausted due to the explosion of internet-connected devices globally
IPv4 cables cannot conduct electricity anymore
IPv4 does not work on modern smartphone screens
8.explanation: IPv6 expands address space to 128 bits, providing virtually inexhaustible addresses.

8.question: How many total bits make up an IPv6 address?
options: 128 bits
256 bits
64 bits
32 bits
8.explanation: IPv6 utilizes 128-bit addresses, written in hexadecimal notation separated by colons.

8.question: What does DNS (Domain Name System) do on the Internet?
options: It translates human-friendly domain names (like example.com) into machine-readable numerical IP addresses
It speeds up computer processor clock rates
It converts paper documents into PDF files
It encrypts credit card numbers in stores
8.explanation: DNS resolves alphanumeric website names into network routing IP addresses.

8.question: Why is DNS often described as the 'phonebook of the Internet'?
options: It looks up and maps hostnames people can remember to the numerical IP addresses computers require to communicate
It lists telephone numbers of software engineers
It sends text messages between smartphones
It prints physical telephone books for tech companies
8.explanation: DNS functions as a distributed directory service mapping names to network addresses.

8.question: What does DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) do on a local network?
options: It formats the hard drive automatically
It checks the computer for software viruses
It cleans dust out of cooling fans
It automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, and default gateways to devices when they connect
8.explanation: DHCP automates network IP address leasing and client configuration.

8.question: What is the difference between a static IP address and a dynamic IP address?
options: A dynamic IP address requires no internet connection
A static IP address only works on laptops
There is no difference between them
A static IP address is permanently assigned and never changes, while a dynamic IP address is leased temporarily and may change
8.explanation: Servers typically require permanent static IPs; client devices use leased dynamic IPs.

8.question: What does TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) guarantee that UDP does not?
options: Exemption from paying internet fees
Reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of data packets via acknowledgments and retransmissions
Instantaneous speed without any delays
Zero bandwidth consumption
8.explanation: TCP establishes connection-oriented sessions guaranteeing lossless, ordered data streams.

8.question: What does UDP (User Datagram Protocol) prioritize over reliability?
options: Military-grade file encryption
Saving files to local hard drives
Speed and low transmission latency, sending packets without handshakes or retransmission delays
Guaranteed delivery of every single byte
8.explanation: UDP is connectionless and lightweight, ideal for time-sensitive voice and video streams.

8.question: Which transport protocol is preferred for real-time video streaming, live voice (VoIP), and online multiplayer games?
options: TCP
UDP
SMTP
FTP
8.explanation: UDP avoids packet-retransmission delays, preventing audio/video stutter in live streams.

8.question: What does HTTP stand for in web communication?
options: Host Terminal Packet
High Transfer Terminal Path
Hyperlink Text Processing
Hypertext Transfer Protocol
8.explanation: HTTP is the foundational application protocol used for transferring web pages.

8.question: What does HTTPS stand for, and why is it essential for modern web browsing?
options: High Technology Protocol Software; it downloads movies faster
Host Terminal Packet Service; it works without Wi-Fi
Hyperlink Text Processing System; it prevents monitor glare
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure; it encrypts communications using TLS/SSL to protect privacy and data integrity
8.explanation: HTTPS secures web sessions against eavesdropping and data tampering.

8.question: What does URL stand for in web navigation?
options: Uniform Resource Locator
Unified Resource Line
Universal Routing Link
Universal Record Link
8.explanation: A URL specifies the global address of a resource on the World Wide Web.

8.question: What is bandwidth in computer networking?
options: The physical thickness of an Ethernet cable
The maximum rate of data transfer across a network path, measured in bits per second (e.g., Mbps or Gbps)
The storage capacity of a hard drive in gigabytes
The frequency of the computer CPU clock
8.explanation: Bandwidth measures the maximum data carrying capacity of a network link.

8.question: What is latency in computer networking?
options: The total size of a downloaded movie
The physical length of a network cable
The time delay it takes for a data packet to travel from its source to its destination across a network (measured in ms)
The number of devices connected to a switch
8.explanation: Latency measures round-trip transit delay (ping) across network hops.

8.question: What does the `ping` utility command do in network diagnostics?
options: It measures the temperature of the router
It reboots the remote server
It tests network connectivity and measures round-trip latency to a target IP address using ICMP echo packets
It deletes temporary internet files
8.explanation: `ping` verifies host reachability and round-trip transmission latency.

8.question: What does the `traceroute` (or `tracert`) network utility do?
options: It measures how fast the mouse moves
It lists installed web browsers
It scans the computer for malware
It traces and displays the exact path of router hops a packet traverses to reach a destination address
8.explanation: `traceroute` diagnoses routing bottlenecks by recording intermediate router hops.

8.question: What is an Ethernet cable (such as Cat6) used for?
options: Transmitting analog audio to headphones
Plugging a computer into a high-voltage wall power outlet
Connecting the monitor directly to the CPU socket
Connecting devices physically to a local area network using twisted-pair copper wiring and RJ-45 connectors
8.explanation: Twisted-pair Ethernet cables deliver reliable, high-speed wired LAN links.

8.question: What is fiber-optic cabling, and why is it used for long-distance internet backbone infrastructure?
options: It uses magnetic radio waves to transmit sound
It is cheaper than copper wires to install in houses
It conducts high-voltage electricity across oceans
It transmits data as pulses of light through flexible glass fibers, providing extremely high bandwidth and immune to EMI
8.explanation: Fiber optics offer massive bandwidth and minimal signal attenuation over vast distances.

8.question: What is a Firewall in computer security?
options: A concrete wall built inside a server room to prevent fires
A hardware or software network security system that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing traffic based on security rules
A physical lock placed on a computer case
An antivirus program that only scans USB flash drives
8.explanation: Firewalls inspect packet traffic to block unauthorized access and cyber threats.

8.question: What is a VPN (Virtual Private Network)?
options: A private physical cable that connects two buildings
A computer monitor that hides screen displays
An encrypted connection over the public Internet that creates a secure, private tunnel between a device and a network
A wireless protocol that connects keyboards to mice
8.explanation: VPNs encrypt network traffic, masking client IP addresses and protecting data privacy.

8.question: What is the difference between the Internet and the World Wide Web (WWW)?
options: The Internet was invented in 2010, while the Web was created in 1950
The Web is hardware and the Internet is software
There is no difference; they are exact synonyms
The Internet is the global physical network of connected computers, while the Web is an information-sharing service built on top of it
8.explanation: The Internet provides network infrastructure; the Web provides hyperlinked documents via HTTP.

8.question: What is the Client-Server network model?
options: A system where devices connect without cables
A network architecture where client devices request resources and centralized servers process and fulfill those requests
A model where computers take turns being turned on
A model where all computers are owned by one person
8.explanation: The client-server architecture separates service consumers from service providers.

8.question: What is a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) network model?
options: A network that operates without internet access
A network where one master computer controls all others
A decentralized network architecture where individual computers share resources and communicate directly as equals without a central server
A network that only connects two smartphones
8.explanation: In P2P networks, every participating node operates as both a client and a server.

9.question: What is malware in computer science?
options: Software used to speed up cooling fans
Malicious software intentionally designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems
Hardware components that have stopped working
Software that translates English into Spanish
9.explanation: Malware encompasses viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, and spyware.

9.question: What is a computer virus?
options: A harmless system file created by the OS
A biological disease that infects human computer operators
A hardware defect in the desktop power supply
Malware that attaches itself to legitimate program files and replicates by inserting its code into other programs when executed
9.explanation: Viruses require user execution of host files to propagate.

9.question: What is a computer worm?
options: A hardware wire connecting the hard drive
A tiny robot that cleans computer cases
A programming language used for robotics
Standalone malware that replicates itself automatically and spreads autonomously across computer networks without needing a host file
9.explanation: Worms self-propagate across network vulnerabilities without human intervention.

9.question: What is a Trojan Horse in cybersecurity?
options: A software program that speeds up internet bandwidth
A wooden statue used to hide computer monitors
Malware disguised as legitimate, desirable software that deceives victims into downloading and installing it
A hardware component made in ancient Greece
9.explanation: Trojans pose as useful utilities while concealing malicious payloads.

9.question: What is ransomware?
options: A backup service that saves files to the cloud
A free antivirus utility provided by the government
Malware that encrypts a victim's personal or organizational files and demands a ransom payment for the decryption key
Software that rents movies over the internet
9.explanation: Ransomware takes files hostage, demanding cryptocurrency payments for recovery.

9.question: What is spyware?
options: A tool that monitors CPU temperature to prevent overheating
A program that cleans physical computer keyboards
Software used by graphic designers to draw 3D models
Malware designed to covertly monitor user activity, record keystrokes, and harvest personal information without consent
9.explanation: Spyware surreptitiously tracks user actions, transmitting data to adversaries.

9.question: What is a keylogger?
options: A tool used by locksmiths to cut metal keys
Surveillance spyware that secretly records every keystroke typed on a keyboard to capture usernames, passwords, and credit cards
A hardware device that cleans keyboard keys
A keyboard shortcut that capitalizes letters
9.explanation: Keyloggers harvest credentials by recording keystroke logs.

9.question: What is phishing in cybersecurity?
options: Searching for music files on the internet
A social engineering attack where attackers impersonate trusted entities via email or websites to steal passwords and sensitive data
Using an optical mouse to click on desktop icons
Catching fish using electronic sonar devices
9.explanation: Phishing lures victims with fraudulent communications into divulging credentials.

9.question: What is spear phishing?
options: A software program that speeds up internet bandwidth
A physical cable that connects two computers
A phishing email sent to millions of people randomly
A targeted, personalized phishing attack tailored specifically to a specific individual or organization using gathered background details
9.explanation: Spear phishing leverages contextual research to deceive specific targets.

9.question: What is social engineering in information security?
options: Designing social media website user interfaces
Psychologically manipulating people into divulging confidential information, bypassing security, or performing risky actions
Building physical desktop computer cases
Writing code for multiplayer video games
9.explanation: Social engineering exploits human trust, urgency, and fear rather than technical flaws.

9.question: What is a Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack?
options: A technique for speeding up computer processors
A method of wiping a hard drive clean
An error caused by unplugging an Ethernet cable
A cyberattack that attempts to make a machine or network resource unavailable to intended users by overwhelming it with flood traffic
9.explanation: DoS attacks saturate target bandwidth or processing capacity, denying legitimate access.

9.question: What is a Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack?
options: A DoS attack launched simultaneously from multiple compromised computers (a botnet) distributed globally across the internet
A computer virus that infects USB thumb drives
An attack executed by a single user typing terminal commands
A physical break-in into a server room
9.explanation: DDoS uses large botnets to amplify attack traffic from thousands of disparate IPs.

9.question: What is a botnet in cybersecurity?
options: A group of robots assembling laptops in a factory
A supercomputer used for studying weather patterns
A collection of helpful chatbots answering customer questions
A network of compromised computers or IoT devices (zombies) controlled remotely by a malicious attacker (botmaster)
9.explanation: Botnets are hijacked device networks marshaled for DDoS, spamming, and crypto mining.

9.question: What is encryption in computer science?
options: Translating Python source code into Spanish
The process of encoding plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a mathematical algorithm and a secret key
Deleting sensitive documents permanently from disk
Compressing a large video file into a ZIP archive
9.explanation: Encryption preserves confidentiality by scrambling data against unauthorized inspection.

9.question: What is decryption?
options: Translating website code into binary
Deleting encrypted files from computer storage
The process of converting encrypted ciphertext back into readable plaintext using the correct cryptographic key
Formatting a solid-state drive
9.explanation: Decryption reconstructs original plaintext from ciphertext using authorized keys.

9.question: What is symmetric encryption?
options: A system that only works on Apple computers
A technique that does not use any keys
A cryptographic system where the EXACT SAME secret key is used to both encrypt and decrypt data (e.g., AES)
A system that uses two completely different keys
9.explanation: Symmetric cryptography shares a single secret key between communicators.

9.question: What is asymmetric (public-key) encryption?
options: A method that requires physical paper keys
A cryptographic system that uses a mathematically linked pair of keys: a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt (e.g., RSA)
An algorithm that never decrypts data
A system that uses one key for all users worldwide
9.explanation: Asymmetric systems publish public keys widely while keeping private keys secret.

9.question: What is a cryptographic hash function (e.g., SHA-256)?
options: A function that scrambles text and easily turns it back
A physical chip located inside the mouse
A mathematical algorithm that transforms input data of any size into a fixed-size string of characters that is deterministic and one-way (irreversible)
A tool used to compress movie files
9.explanation: Hash functions produce unique fixed-length digests that cannot be reversed.

9.question: Why do secure databases store passwords as cryptographic hashes rather than plaintext?
options: Because hashes allow passwords to be viewed by any employee
If the database is stolen or compromised, attackers cannot directly read the actual plaintext passwords
Because computers cannot store plaintext words
Because hashed passwords take up more disk space
9.explanation: Storing hashes prevents credential exposure during database breaches.

9.question: What is salting in password hashing security?
options: Adding numbers to a password when typing it
Adding random data (salt) to a password before hashing it to ensure identical passwords produce different hash values, defeating rainbow tables
Storing passwords in a refrigerator
Pouring physical salt into computer cooling fans
9.explanation: Salting prevents precomputed dictionary lookup and rainbow table attacks.

9.question: What is Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA / 2FA)?
options: Using two different web browsers to sign into email
Changing computer passwords every single day
A security verification method requiring users to provide two or more distinct authentication factors before granting account access
Typing the exact same password two times in a row
9.explanation: MFA combines factors across knowledge, possession, and inherence.

9.question: Which of the following represents 'something you have' in multi-factor authentication?
options: Your mother's maiden name
A one-time verification code sent to your smartphone authenticator app or a physical security key
Your fingerprint or facial recognition scan
Your secret memorized account password
9.explanation: Authenticator apps, hardware tokens, and smart cards represent possession factors.

9.question: Which of the following represents 'something you are' in authentication?
options: A physical security key
A memorized password
A PIN number
A biometric scan such as fingerprint, facial recognition, or retina scan
9.explanation: Biometrics authenticate innate physiological traits.

9.question: Which of the following represents 'something you know' in authentication?
options: A smart card badge
A smartphone token
A password, passphrase, or PIN number
A fingerprint scan
9.explanation: Knowledge factors rely on confidential memorized data.

9.question: What is a password manager?
options: A website that shares passwords with the public
A person whose job is to memorize passwords for employees
A physical notepad left on a desktop computer desk
A software application that securely generates, encrypts, and stores unique, complex passwords for all your online accounts
9.explanation: Password managers maintain encrypted vaults unlocked by a single master passphrase.

9.question: What makes a password strong and resilient against brute-force attacks?
options: Using your birthdate and first name
Sufficient length (14+ characters), combining uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols without dictionary words or personal info
Using the word 'password123'
Using a single short dictionary word
9.explanation: High character entropy and length exponentially expand brute-force search spaces.

9.question: What is a zero-day vulnerability in cybersecurity?
options: A vulnerability that only exists for zero seconds
A software bug that occurs on New Year's Day
A defect that causes zero harm to computer systems
A software security flaw that is unknown to the software vendor, leaving zero days for a patch before potential exploitation
9.explanation: Zero-days present critical risk because no vendor defenses or patches yet exist.

9.question: What is a software security patch?
options: A physical sticker placed over a laptop webcam
A replacement cooling fan for a noisy desktop
An update released by software developers to fix known security vulnerabilities, bugs, and operational flaws
A piece of cloth used to clean computer monitors
9.explanation: Patches remediate discovered flaws to prevent exploit weaponization.

9.question: Why is prompt installation of operating system and software security updates critical?
options: It wipes the computer hard drive clean
It increases the brightness of the screen display
It makes the computer physically lighter in weight
It closes known security vulnerabilities before malicious hackers can exploit them to compromise your computer
9.explanation: Delayed patching leaves systems exposed to automated exploit kits targeting known flaws.

9.question: What is a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack?
options: A virus that infects middle-aged computers
A physical person standing between two computer desks
A computer monitor placed between two keyboards
An attack where the adversary secretly intercepts and potentially alters communications between two parties who believe they are communicating directly
9.explanation: MitM attackers eavesdrop on or manipulate session traffic on unsecured networks.

9.question: Why is entering passwords on public, unencrypted Wi-Fi networks risky without a VPN or HTTPS?
options: Public Wi-Fi charges $50 per password typed
Public Wi-Fi automatically deletes all user files
Public Wi-Fi causes smartphone batteries to explode
Attackers on the same network can use packet sniffers to intercept unencrypted transmission traffic and capture credentials
9.explanation: Unsecured networks expose unencrypted packets to eavesdropping on the local broadcast domain.

9.question: What is identity theft?
options: Borrowing a friend's textbook with permission
Wearing a costume to a school masquerade party
Forgetting your computer login password
The illegal acquisition and fraudulent use of another person's personal data (e.g., Social Security number, name) for financial gain
9.explanation: Identity theft enables fraudulent account openings, loan applications, and criminal impersonation.

9.question: What is the Principle of Least Privilege in security architecture?
options: Giving every employee full administrator access to all servers
Granting users and programs only the minimum access levels and permissions necessary to perform their specific tasks
Refusing to allow employees to use computer mice
Shutting down the network every weekend
9.explanation: Least privilege limits potential collateral damage from compromised accounts or rogue scripts.

9.question: What is a data breach?
options: An employee forgetting their login password
An operating system installing an authorized update
A security incident where confidential, sensitive, or protected data is copied, transmitted, viewed, or stolen by an unauthorized individual
A computer monitor turning off to save power
9.explanation: Breaches expose confidential customer records, intellectual property, or trade secrets.

9.question: What is social media digital footprint?
options: The trail of personal data, browsing history, posts, comments, and photos left behind by a user's digital activity online
The physical size of a desktop computer case
A smudge left by fingers on a touchscreen
The electricity consumed by a server room
9.explanation: Digital footprints persist across web archives, search engines, and commercial data brokers.

9.question: What are HTTP cookies in web browsers?
options: Small text files stored on a user's computer by websites to remember login states, site preferences, and track browsing sessions
Computer viruses that corrupt hard drives
Sweet baked snacks eaten while programming
Hardware chips inside the computer mouse
9.explanation: Cookies preserve session state and tracking tokens between HTTP requests.

9.question: What is third-party tracking on the web?
options: When three people share a single computer
When external ad networks or analytics services collect browsing history across multiple unrelated websites to build user advertising profiles
When a website saves your password securely
When your computer downloads an operating system update
9.explanation: Third-party trackers monitor cross-site behavior to serve targeted programmatic ads.

9.question: What is the purpose of private browsing mode (Incognito mode) in web browsers?
options: It provides military-grade encryption for all files
It prevents websites from tracking your IP address
It makes the user 100% invisible to internet service providers and employers
It prevents the browser from saving local browsing history, cookies, and temporary site data on the local device after the session closes
9.explanation: Private browsing keeps local device history clean but does not conceal activity from ISPs or sites.

9.question: What is ethical hacking (white-hat hacking)?
options: Breaking into school computers to change grades
Spreading computer viruses to test antivirus software
Hacking into bank servers to steal money for charity
Authorized penetration testing performed to identify and remediate security vulnerabilities before malicious actors exploit them
9.explanation: White-hat professionals evaluate system defenses legally under explicit rules of engagement.

9.question: What is a black-hat hacker?
options: An individual who penetrates computer systems without authorization with malicious intent, personal financial gain, or disruption
A programmer who writes open-source code
A software engineer who wears dark clothing
A computer technician who repairs laptop hardware
9.explanation: Black-hat hackers exploit vulnerabilities illicitly for profit, extortion, or espionage.

9.question: What is a red flag in a suspicious phishing email message?
options: An email scheduling a meeting during normal school hours
An email that contains zero links or attachments
Generic greetings, urgent threats of account closure, mismatched sender domain addresses, and unexpected hyperlinks or attachments
An email sent from an official verified school address
9.explanation: Urgency, generic salutations, and spoofed domains are hallmarks of phishing lures.

9.question: What is ransomware extortion through data exfiltration (double extortion)?
options: Deleting all files twice to ensure they are gone
Charging double the normal price for software
Asking for payment in two different currencies
Stealing sensitive corporate data before encrypting it, and threatening to leak it publicly if the ransom is not paid
9.explanation: Double extortion pressures victims by threatening public disclosure of stolen IP or customer data.

9.question: What is an air-gapped computer?
options: A computer that is physically isolated and has no network interfaces connecting it to the Internet or any other network
A laptop used outdoors in the fresh air
A computer cooled by compressed air fans
A computer monitor with holes drilled in the frame
9.explanation: Air gaps isolate high-security computers from external remote network attacks.

9.question: What is a honeypot in cybersecurity?
options: A jar of honey placed inside a server room
A virus that attracts sweet files
A decoy system or server set up intentionally to lure attackers, detect intrusions, and study their attack methods
A pleasant sound played when logging in
9.explanation: Honeypots bait attackers to isolate attack vectors without risking production systems.

9.question: What does GDPR stand for in international data privacy regulations?
options: Global Digital Privacy Rule
General Data Protection Regulation
Government Data Protection Registry
General Device Programming Requirement
9.explanation: GDPR is the European Union's comprehensive data privacy and protection regulation.

9.question: What is COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act) in US federal law?
options: A law requiring children to learn coding in school
A law regulating video game pricing
A law that provides free laptops to students
A law that protects the personal information of children under 13 by requiring parental consent for data collection
9.explanation: COPPA regulates commercial websites and apps collecting personal data from kids under 13.

9.question: What is a DDoS mitigation service (such as Cloudflare)?
options: A hardware device that replaces computer monitors
A tool for editing video files
A program that cleans dust from cooling fans
A cloud security service that absorbs and filters massive malicious flood traffic before it reaches the origin web server
9.explanation: DDoS mitigation proxies and absorbs multi-gigabit traffic spikes via global anycast networks.

9.question: What is two-way SSL/TLS authentication?
options: Installing two web browsers on the desktop
Both the client and the server authenticate each other using digital certificates, establishing a mutual trust relationship
Using two different passwords to open an account
Connecting two computers with an Ethernet cable
9.explanation: Mutual TLS (mTLS) validates cryptographic identity on both ends of a secure connection.

9.question: What is responsible disclosure in cybersecurity research?
options: Posting live software exploits on social media immediately
Selling confidential user passwords on the dark web
Privately reporting security vulnerabilities to the software vendor and providing reasonable time to patch before public release
Refusing to report bugs to software companies
9.explanation: Responsible disclosure mitigates threats before exposing end users to zero-day exploits.

9.question: Why is user awareness and security education considered the most vital layer of cybersecurity defense?
options: Because computers cannot run antivirus software
Because hardware cables fail every day
Human error and social engineering are the primary vectors exploited by cybercriminals to bypass technological security controls
Because software programs never have bugs
9.explanation: Education transforms human users from the weakest security link into an active defensive perimeter.

10.question: What is artificial intelligence (AI)?
options: The capability of computational systems to perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as learning and problem-solving
A computer screen displaying colorful animations
A mechanical robot with biological muscles
A high-speed wireless home internet router
10.explanation: AI enables machines to learn, reason, infer, and perceive from data.

10.question: What is machine learning (ML)?
options: Cleaning computer keyboards with compressed air
Manually typing millions of lines of code
A branch of AI focused on building algorithms that learn from data and improve their performance over time without explicit programming
A factory assembly line building laptops
10.explanation: ML discovers predictive patterns from training datasets autonomously.

10.question: What is deep learning in artificial intelligence?
options: Memorizing binary numbers from 0 to 1,000
Reading thick computer science textbooks
A subset of machine learning based on artificial neural networks with multiple representation layers (deep architectures)
Learning that takes place deep underwater
10.explanation: Deep learning leverages multi-layer neural networks for complex perceptual tasks.

10.question: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)?
options: A programming language that uses numbers only
A hardware processor with voice speakers
A tool that translates English into binary code
The branch of AI concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language
10.explanation: NLP powers machine translation, voice assistants, sentiment analysis, and LLMs.

10.question: What is Computer Vision in artificial intelligence?
options: The field of AI that trains computers to interpret and understand the visual world from digital images and videos
A webcam connected via a USB cable
A pair of glasses worn by software engineers
A high-resolution computer monitor display
10.explanation: Computer vision extracts high-level semantic insights from digital pixels and video feeds.

10.question: What is an autonomous vehicle (self-driving car)?
options: A car that runs on electricity instead of gas
A car that is controlled by a remote control toy
A car that can only drive in straight lines
A vehicle capable of sensing its environment and navigating without human operational input using sensors, cameras, and AI
10.explanation: Autonomous vehicles integrate lidar, radar, computer vision, and deep learning.

10.question: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?
options: A global network of physical devices embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity to collect and exchange data (e.g., smart thermostats)
A website that sells computer components online
A physical cable that connects home appliances
A new programming language created for supercomputers
10.explanation: IoT connects everyday consumer and industrial appliances into telemetry networks.

10.question: What is edge computing?
options: Computing done at the edge of a desk
Processing data locally near the source of generation (such as on an IoT device or local gateway) rather than relying exclusively on a distant cloud
Using computers during severe weather
A type of graphics rendering algorithm
10.explanation: Edge computing reduces latency and bandwidth demands by computing locally.

10.question: What is cloud computing?
options: Storing files directly inside the computer monitor
A wireless protocol that connects keyboards to mice
Operating computers exclusively on rainy days
The on-demand delivery of compute power, database storage, applications, and other IT resources via the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing
10.explanation: Cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP) provide scalable virtualized infrastructure.

10.question: What does SaaS stand for in cloud service models?
options: Software as a Service (e.g., Google Docs, Microsoft 365)
Storage and Application Server
System as a Software
Serial Access Software
10.explanation: SaaS delivers end-user applications directly over web browsers without local installation.

10.question: What does IaaS stand for in cloud computing?
options: Integrated Array Service
Internet as a Software
Infrastructure as a Service (e.g., virtual servers, raw storage, networks)
Interactive Application System
10.explanation: IaaS rents fundamental compute, storage, and networking building blocks.

10.question: What does PaaS stand for in cloud platforms?
options: Personal Application System
Packet and Array Server
Platform as a Service (e.g., development environments, databases, runtime engines)
Program as a Service
10.explanation: PaaS provides developers with ready-to-use application deployment frameworks.

10.question: What is blockchain technology?
options: A computer chip that replaces the motherboard
A chain used to lock desktop computers to desks
A decentralized, distributed public ledger that records transactions across a network of computers in tamper-resistant chronological blocks
A software program that speeds up internet downloads
10.explanation: Blockchains enforce trust and data immutability through cryptographic consensus.

10.question: What is a smart contract in blockchain platforms (such as Ethereum)?
options: A legal document signed with a digital pen
Self-executing code stored on a blockchain that automatically runs and enforces terms when predetermined conditions are met
A loan application approved by a bank manager
A phone contract that has unlimited internet data
10.explanation: Smart contracts automate decentralized agreements without intermediaries.

10.question: What is cryptocurrency?
options: A paper check written by a commercial bank
A plastic debit card backed by FDIC insurance
A digital or virtual currency that is secured by cryptography and operates on decentralized networks without central bank oversight
A physical gold coin minted by the federal government
10.explanation: Cryptocurrencies (e.g., Bitcoin) enable trustless peer-to-peer value transfer.

10.question: What is quantum computing?
options: Computing technology based on the principles of quantum mechanics (superposition and entanglement) to perform calculations intractable for classical computers
Computing using small plastic beads
Connecting monitors with optical glass
Running software without any electricity
10.explanation: Quantum computers utilize qubits that exist in superpositions of 0 and 1 simultaneously.

10.question: What is a qubit (quantum bit)?
options: A bit that is sent over a wireless network
A bit that can never be saved to disk
The basic unit of quantum information, capable of representing 0, 1, or any quantum superposition of both states at once
A bit that has been compressed in a ZIP file
10.explanation: Qubits provide exponential parallel calculation state spaces.

10.question: What is virtual reality (VR)?
options: A standard computer game played with a mouse
An immersive, computer-generated simulation of a three-dimensional environment that users can interact with using headsets and motion sensors
A high-definition television broadcast
A video recorded on a smartphone camera
10.explanation: VR replaces the user's physical visual surroundings with synthetic digital worlds.

10.question: What is augmented reality (AR)?
options: A printed photograph in a magazine
A computer monitor with high screen brightness
An interactive experience where digital information, images, and sounds are superimposed onto the real-world physical environment (e.g., Pokémon GO)
A virtual world that completely blocks out the real world
10.explanation: AR overlays digital contextual data onto real-world sensory inputs.

10.question: What is 3D printing (additive manufacturing)?
options: Printing photographs on glossy photo paper
The process of creating three-dimensional solid physical objects from a digital CAD file by depositing successive layers of material
A laser printer that prints text in color
A scanner that converts documents into PDFs
10.explanation: Additive manufacturing builds physical geometry layer by layer from digital models.

10.question: What is big data in computer science and industry?
options: Extremely large, complex, and rapidly growing datasets characterized by the '3 Vs': Volume, Velocity, and Variety
A computer monitor with a huge screen display
A physical hard drive that weighs 50 pounds
A spreadsheet that contains ten rows of numbers
10.explanation: Big data encompasses datasets whose scale exceeds traditional relational database handling.

10.question: What is algorithmic bias in machine learning?
options: An error caused by a computer battery dying
Systematic and repeatable errors in an AI system that create unfair outcomes, such as privileging one group over another due to biased training data
The preference of programmers for a specific language
A hardware defect in the computer cooling fan
10.explanation: Biased training datasets can perpetuate and amplify societal historical inequities.

10.question: What is facial recognition technology, and what ethical concerns surround its deployment?
options: A tool that cleans computer monitors
A screen that changes colors automatically
A software program that plays music
AI that identifies individuals from facial geometry; concerns include mass surveillance, privacy erosion, and racial/demographic accuracy disparities
10.explanation: Facial recognition poses civil liberties risks regarding surveillance and biased misidentification.

10.question: What is a Deepfake in digital media?
options: Synthetic media in which a person's likeness, face, or voice is realistically replaced with someone else's using deep learning AI models
A text document translated into Spanish
A computer game with realistic graphics
An image that has been cropped in Photoshop
10.explanation: Deepfakes present severe challenges regarding disinformation, fraud, and defamation.

10.question: What is the Digital Divide?
options: The socioeconomic gap between demographic groups and regions that have access to modern information technology and those that do not
The distance between a monitor and a keyboard
A physical wall built inside computer factories
The difference in price between desktops and laptops
10.explanation: The digital divide restricts educational and economic opportunity for underserved populations.

10.question: What is digital citizenship?
options: A certificate awarded to computer scientists
The responsible, ethical, safe, and respectful use of technology, digital communications, and internet resources
A permit required to open a social media account
A passport that allows programmers to travel
10.explanation: Digital citizenship teaches media literacy, respectful discourse, and cyber safety.

10.question: What is e-waste (electronic waste)?
options: Temporary files deleted from the desktop recycle bin
Spam emails sent across the internet
Discarded electrical and electronic devices (like old smartphones and computers) that contain hazardous heavy metals that pollute ecosystems
The heat generated by laptop cooling fans
10.explanation: E-waste contains lead, mercury, and cadmium, requiring certified recycling management.

10.question: What is green computing (sustainable IT)?
options: The environmentally responsible and eco-friendly design, manufacturing, use, and disposal of computers and technological infrastructure
Running computers on lawns and in parks
Painting computer desktop towers green
A software program that waters plants
10.explanation: Green computing minimizes carbon footprints through energy-efficient hardware and recycling.

10.question: What is intellectual property (IP) in technology?
options: The plastic packaging used to ship electronics
The electricity that powers server rooms
Legal rights protecting creations of the human mind, including software source code, algorithms, patents, and digital content
Physical computer hardware in a warehouse
10.explanation: IP frameworks (patents, copyrights, trademarks) safeguard commercial innovations.

10.question: What does copyright protect in computer software development?
options: Mathematical ideas and abstract algorithm concepts
The physical silicon chips inside a computer
The clock speed of the processor
The original creative expression of source code, documentation, and graphical user interface assets
10.explanation: Copyright automatically protects original code expressions against unauthorized copying.

10.question: What does a patent protect in computing technology?
options: A student's high school diploma
A company's brand logo and slogan
A creative poem written in a text file
Novel, non-obvious, and useful inventions, hardware mechanisms, and technical operational processes for a limited period (e.g., 20 years)
10.explanation: Patents grant exclusive temporary monopoly rights to commercialize technical inventions.

10.question: What is a software license agreement (EULA)?
options: A driver's license required to operate a PC
A receipt given after buying a laptop
A legally binding contract between a software author/publisher and the end user specifying terms, rights, and restrictions on usage
A diploma awarded to software developers
10.explanation: EULAs define permitted installations, redistribution limits, and warranty disclaimers.

10.question: What is the General Public License (GNU GPL) in open source?
options: A license that charges $100 per user
A proprietary license that forbids viewing code
A copyleft open-source license that guarantees users the freedom to run, study, share, and modify software, requiring derivative works to remain open
A software tool that formats hard drives
10.explanation: The GPL ensures that open-source software and its derivatives remain perpetually free and open.

10.question: What is the MIT License in open-source software?
options: A license that requires users to attend MIT university
A short, highly permissive open-source license that allows users to do virtually anything with the code as long as original copyright notices are retained
A government law that regulates computers
A license that strictly forbids commercial use
10.explanation: The MIT license grants broad commercial and personal freedoms with minimal restrictions.

10.question: What is Creative Commons (CC)?
options: A commercial software company selling fonts
A non-profit organization that provides standardized, flexible copyright licenses enabling creators to share educational content and digital media legally
An international court that regulates trade
A government agency that collects sales taxes
10.explanation: Creative Commons allows creators to grant public permissions for creative works.

10.question: What is net neutrality?
options: A law requiring all internet content to be free
The principle that Internet Service Providers (ISPs) must treat all internet data and communications equally, without blocking, throttling, or paid prioritization
A rule that prevents people from using Wi-Fi
A technique for speeding up computer processors
10.explanation: Net neutrality forbids ISPs from discriminating against specific content, websites, or apps.

10.question: What is cybersecurity ethics?
options: Refusing to tell companies about security flaws
Selling stolen passwords on the dark web
The moral principles guiding the conduct of security professionals regarding privacy, responsible disclosure, and authorized testing
Creating computer viruses to test antivirus tools
10.explanation: Cyber ethics ensures that technical security skills are exercised responsibly and lawfully.

10.question: What is the impact of automation and AI on the global workforce?
options: It permanently eliminates the need for human communication
It makes all programming languages obsolete
It replaces all computer hardware with paper notebooks
It automates routine cognitive and physical tasks, transforming occupational roles and creating high demand for technical, analytical, and creative skills
10.explanation: Automation reshapes economies, displacing routine tasks while elevating demand for analytical skills.

10.question: What is computational biology / bioinformatics?
options: Building computers made out of living plants
The application of computer science, data science, and algorithms to understand biological systems, genetics, and molecular structures
Cleaning computer keyboards with soap
A software program that plays bird sounds
10.explanation: Bioinformatics processes massive genomic datasets (DNA sequencing, protein folding).

10.question: What is fintech (financial technology)?
options: A physical bank building made of steel
A software program that tracks gym workouts
The application of computer software, mobile devices, and cloud algorithms to modernize and automate financial and banking services
A coin made of plastic instead of copper
10.explanation: Fintech encompasses mobile payments, robo-advising, blockchain, and automated lending.

10.question: What is assistive technology in computing?
options: A software program that plays computer games
A tool that cleans computer monitors
A printer that prints ten pages per minute
Hardware and software designed to improve, maintain, or enhance the functional capabilities of individuals with disabilities (e.g., screen readers)
10.explanation: Assistive technology (screen readers, eye-tracking, braille displays) fosters digital accessibility.

10.question: What is Web Accessibility (a11y) and the WCAG standard?
options: Designing websites and digital content so that people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate, and interact with them effectively
Making sure websites load in under one second
Translating all web pages into Latin
Making websites display bright neon colors
10.explanation: WCAG guidelines mandate accessible color contrast, screen reader semantics, and keyboard navigation.

10.question: What is telemetry in modern software and operating systems?
options: The automated remote collection and transmission of software diagnostic, performance, and usage data back to developers
A telephone call between computer engineers
A telescope that watches space satellites
A television show about computer science
10.explanation: Telemetry reports crash logs and feature usage to guide performance optimization.

10.question: What is smart infrastructure in modern urban planning?
options: Installing more parking meters on streets
Integrating IoT sensors, data networks, and AI algorithms into city infrastructure (e.g., adaptive traffic lights, water monitoring)
Paving roads with white cement
Building taller concrete skyscrapers
10.explanation: Smart infrastructure optimizes resource utilization, safety, and transit flow.

10.question: What is high-performance computing (HPC)?
options: A computer monitor with a curved screen
A smartphone that plays music loudly
A laptop that has a colorful keyboard
Aggregating computing power through clusters of networked computers to perform complex scientific and engineering simulations
10.explanation: HPC clusters run massive parallel simulations in physics, climate, and molecular dynamics.

10.question: What is wearable technology (wearables)?
options: Shoes with flashing LED battery lights
Clothing made of physical metal wires
Electronic devices embedded with microcontrollers and sensors designed to be worn comfortably on the human body (e.g., smartwatches, fitness bands)
A backpack used to carry desktop PCs
10.explanation: Wearables track biometric health telemetry and deliver real-time notifications.

10.question: What is data sovereignty in international law?
options: The legal concept that digital data is subject to the laws and governance of the nation in which it is physically stored or collected
A tax placed on downloading digital music
A law that gives computers citizenship rights
The rule that all data must be deleted every year
10.explanation: Data sovereignty mandates that cloud providers comply with local jurisdiction privacy regulations.

10.question: What is the dark web?
options: A website that uses black background colors
The internet when turned off during the night
A hidden collective of internet sites accessible only through specialized encrypted browsers (like Tor) that mask user and server identities
A social media platform for nighttime workers
10.explanation: The dark web uses layered onion routing to ensure anonymity for both publishers and visitors.

10.question: What is digital forensics?
options: Repairing cracked smartphone screens
The scientific recovery, preservation, and analysis of evidence found in computers and digital storage devices for legal proceedings
Designing graphics for video games
Writing code for automated web bots
10.explanation: Digital forensics investigates cybercrimes, tracking digital breadcrumbs and memory artifacts.

10.question: Why does the study of computer science inspire lifelong curiosity and continuous learning?
options: Because computers are redesigned with different electricity every year
Computing technologies, programming paradigms, and digital tools evolve rapidly, constantly creating new frontiers for human innovation and problem-solving
Because computer science degrees expire after six months
Because old computer code stops working after one year
10.explanation: Computer science empowers lifelong learners to invent tools that solve pressing global challenges.
